title: Learning Motion-Appearance Coupling Priors for Solving Video Inverse Problems
claim: Adding a learned prior over motion-appearance coupling yields reconstructions much closer to ground truth than standard consistency baselines.
layout: 1 row of 5 image panels, left-to-right, PSNR overlaid on each
description: A single horizontal strip of five square video frames, all showing the same washed-out, hazy outdoor scene. A person stands on a ladder operating a camera, with a bush and hills behind and a bright sky above. The leftmost frame is the ground truth and has no number. The other four are reconstructions from a 4x undersampled compressive-sensing measurement, with PSNR values in white text at the bottom-left: 28.1 dB, 28.3 dB, 40.21 dB, and 44.50 dB. The first two (noise warping and a baseline) show heavy haze, ghosting and blur around the figure. The third (photometric consistency) is cleaner. The rightmost (ours) looks nearly identical to the ground truth and has the highest PSNR. The panel titles are cropped off at the top. The eye goes to the PSNR labels and the visible quality jump from left to right.
caption: Reconstruction with a motion-appearance coupling prior outperforms noise warping and photometric consistency baselines. We consider the problem of reconstructing a video from a 4× undersampled dynamic compressive sensing problem. We use the pretrained ADM image diffusion model [DN21] and apply integral noise warping or photometric consistency adapted from HIWYN [Cha+24] and MGLD [Yan+24]. Integral noise warping provides no consistent improvement for this problem. Minimizing a confidence-weighted photometric loss during sampling improves results, but is outperformed by our proposed approach of reconstructing with a prior trained on motion-appearance coupling.
abstract: Reconstructing video from degraded measurements requires priors that capture both frame appearance and temporal dynamics. Many recent approaches combine pretrained image diffusion priors with motion guidance, sidestepping the costs of training large video models. Temporal consistency is often enforced via photometric losses or warping-based constraints, which implicitly assume that motion explains frame-to-frame or latent-to-latent changes up to small deviations, an assumption that fails under occlusions, lighting changes, and non-rigid deformation. In this paper, we propose to learn the coupling between motion and frame appearance as a generative prior. We learn the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals with a conditional diffusion model and use it to regularize reconstruction in video inverse problems. Our motion-appearance prior acts as a plug-in regularizer for diffusion-based video reconstruction, preserving the benefits of image diffusion models while remaining compatible with existing appearance regularization techniques. Experiments on dynamic video inverse problems show that reconstruction with a learnt motion-appearance coupling prior outperforms photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines, and that the approach also transfers to cardiac MRI reconstruction.
